title: Love God, Serve Man -- Ch. 9: Bukas Loob sa Diyos: Called to Evangelize
keywords: Reform your lives and believe in the gospel
Second Plenary Council of the Philippines
Council of the Laity of the Philippines
primary_topics: Chapter 9 of 'Love God, Serve Man' -- the reflection CJP delivered on February 23, 1994 before a prayer meeting of the Bukas Loob Sa Diyos Catholic Covenant Community at the Philippine International Convention Center, built on Mark 1:15's command to reform our lives and believe in the gospel.

His 'three Cs of reformation' -- contrition, conversion and Christianization, or repentance, transformation and evangelization -- presented not as graduated stages but as overlapping movements a mature Christian lives at once.

The 'signs of the times' he reads for BLD: the conscription of four of its members into PCP II, Sonny de los Reyes's election and reelection as president of the Council of the Laity of the Philippines, the emergence of BLD's new vision-charism-mission, and his own reluctant call to be a Servant Leader.

The call to Christianize the 'invisible laity': with priests pastoring 40,000 to 50,000 parishioners each and only about 2 percent of Catholics active, some 50 million Filipinos remain unchurched, uninvolved and untouched by the parish -- the challenge he lays on his hearers.
sub_topics: The parable of Pancracio: a well-educated, hard-working young man who became a multi-millionaire at 35, crashed his brand-new BMW, and in a coma at the ICU begged Mr. Death for more time, confessing he had never prayed, never minded his neighbor and did not even know the Commandments.

Mr. Death's bargain and its collection: the promise of warnings before the next visit; Pancracio's relapse into wealth, women and wine by 45; and Mr. Death's retort that the eyeglasses, the dentures, the uric acid, the cholesterol and the blood sugar over 300 were warning enough.

The application: there is a part of Pancracio in all of us -- mischievous, procrastinating, rationalizing and sinful -- but the Lord's exhortation is more than a warning, it is an order, reinforced by Mark 13's command to be constantly on the watch since no one knows the day or the hour.

Repentance or contrition defined: being sincerely sorry, admitting our faults and facing the consequences before a forgiving rather than a vengeful God, with the sacrament of reconciliation as the Church's way to total forgiveness of mortal sin and BLD members urged to confess monthly.

Repentance as daily practice for the renewed: part of daily prayer, of evening reflections and of all-day conversation with the Lord, cleansing spiritually, physically and psychologically, since prayer without repentance is without power and hard-heartedness blocks the Lord's healing grace.

The red-light illustration: real contrition means hating sin itself rather than merely fearing hell's fury, as some stop at a red light from fear of the policeman while others stop because they believe in orderly traffic.

Restitution as the proof of contrition: saying sorry is not enough -- a thief must return what he took and one who injures another must pay the medical expenses -- as Zacchaeus gave half his belongings to the poor and repaid fourfold those he had defrauded.

Transformation or conversion: a firm commitment never to sin again and a vow to follow Jesus in words, thoughts and actions -- a call to metanoia, a day-to-day grinding, grasping and following of Christ, usually lifelong but sometimes instantaneous, as with St. Paul on the road to Damascus, St. Augustine, and the repentant thief.

Evangelization or Christianization: once converted we begin to glow, people notice the change in lifestyle, language, relationships, actions and habits, and we become unconscious witnesses -- the lamp that cannot be hidden of Matthew 5.

The social reach of evangelization: we cannot go to heaven alone, we are called to promote human development, break the yoke of the poor, fight injustice, liberate man from bigotry and work for peace, since at the final judgment God will ask not about bankbooks, Mercedeses or PhDs but what we did for the least of our brethren.

The crowning glory: evangelization fulfilled when the evangelized becomes the evangelizer, the student the teacher, the lamb the shepherd -- and, paraphrasing Santa Teresa of Avila, when the evangelized become Christ to others.

PCP II as the battle cry: evangelization must build up the Church yet not stop there, seeking to transform the whole fabric of society, because while the majority are Catholics and the churches are filled on Sundays, 'our society remains a sick society.'

The transformation of BLD itself: founded ten years earlier, beginning with the Marriage Encounter, the Life in the Spirit Seminar and the Family Encounter, then growth and discipleship programs, and two years ago turning outward to the larger Church's renewed evangelization.

The four signs of the times: the conscription of Sonny de los Reyes, Robert Corpus, Pat Menzon and himself into PCP II in early 1991 with no other lay organization equally represented; Sonny's election in 1991 and reelection in 1993 to head the Council of the Laity; the emergence of BLD's vision-charism-mission for the family, basic ecclesial communities and parishes, for breaking the yoke of poverty and for raising an army of prayer warriors; and the personal sign of his own calling.

His personal account of resistance: how he and Leni had decided to be just ordinary members, leading no prayer meeting, declining to share at MEs and LSS, not teaching and going on leave as stewards -- and how the Lord's call was so pervading and deafening that after all the running away all he could answer was 'Here I am Lord.'

The statistics of the unchurched: priests ministering to 40,000 to 50,000 parishioners; only 2 percent of Catholics active and 10 percent regular churchgoers, so that of 56 million Filipino Catholics about a million are active and five million churchgoing; most communicants women, the 'highly audible-visible laity,' most men the 'reluctant laity,' and 88 percent or about 50 million the 'invisible laity.'

The closing commission: the Lord's reward for BLD's good work is more hard work, under the Great Commission of Matthew 28 to make disciples of all nations, with the promise that He is with them until the end of the world.

notable_anecdotes: The Pancracio parable: the 35-year-old multi-millionaire who crashed his brand-new BMW, met Mr. Death in a sinister black robe at his Makati Medical Center door, and pleaded for another chance because he had neglected God and did not even know the Commandments.

Mr. Death's accounting: told he had been given sufficient warning -- the eyeglasses for diminished eyesight, the new dentures for loosened teeth, the sky-flying uric acid and cholesterol, the blood sugar above 300 -- at the second visit after an evening of merrymaking.
The red light: his image of two drivers, one stopping from fear of the policeman and the other because he believes in orderly traffic, used to distinguish fear of punishment from hatred of sin.

The conscription into PCP II: he recalls that he, Sonny de los Reyes, Robert Corpus and Pat Menzon were drafted into the council in early 1991, and that no other lay organization had an equal number of lay members in that historic body.

His two years of hiding: he and Leni resolved to be ordinary members, leading no prayer meeting, declining to share at the encounters, refusing to teach and going on leave as stewards -- until the call grew so deafening that he could only answer 'Here I am Lord.'
The song at judgment: he quotes the anointed song sung at their prayer meetings -- 'We fought the fight, we ran the race' -- and its line that only what we have done for Christ will last eternally.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 9 of 'Love God, Serve Man' records the reflection Atty. Artemio V. Panganiban delivered on February 23, 1994 before a prayer meeting of the Bukas Loob Sa Diyos Catholic Covenant Community at the Philippine International Convention Center, where he served on the Council of Servant Leaders and chaired the BLD Foundation. Taking Mark 1:15 as his text, he opens with the parable of Pancracio, a hard-working young man who became a multi-millionaire at 35, crashed his new BMW, and in a coma begged Mr. Death for more time, confessing he had never prayed and did not know the Commandments; granted a reprieve and the promise of warning, he relapsed into wealth, women and wine, and at 45 was told that the eyeglasses, the dentures, the soaring uric acid and cholesterol and the blood sugar above 300 had been warning enough. Since a part of Pancracio lurks in everyone, he says, the Lord's command to reform is not a warning but an order. He then sets out his three Cs of reformation. Contrition means being sincerely sorry, facing the consequences and confessing before a forgiving God; it is a daily practice for the renewed, since prayer without repentance is without power; and it means hating sin itself, as one driver stops at a red light from conviction and another only from fear of the policeman. It also requires restitution, as Zacchaeus repaid fourfold. Conversion is the firm commitment never to sin again and the vow to follow Jesus -- a call to metanoia usually lifelong but sometimes instant, as with St. Paul, St. Augustine and the repentant thief. Evangelization follows as the converted begin to glow and become unconscious witnesses, the lamp that cannot be hidden; and because we cannot go to heaven alone, it reaches to human development, the yoke of the poor, injustice and peace, judged at the last by what was done for the least of our brethren. Quoting PCP II that evangelization must transform the whole fabric of society because 'our society remains a sick society,' he reads four signs of the times for BLD -- four of its members drafted into PCP II, Sonny de los Reyes's election to head the Council of the Laity, the community's new vision-charism-mission, and his own reluctant call after two years of hiding, answered at last with 'Here I am Lord.' He closes on the statistics of the unchurched: only about a million of 56 million Filipino Catholics are active, 88 percent being the 'invisible laity,' so the Lord's reward for BLD's past work is more hard work under the Great Commission.
